Formulation:
- The patient presents with upper respiratory symptoms including dry cough (every 20-30 minutes), constant green nasal discharge, mild systemic viral symptoms (subjective feeling hot and chilly, mild muscle aches), and no severe respiratory distress signs.  
- Relevant chronic medical conditions (diabetes and hypertension) increase infection risk though recent blood tests suggest stable diabetes control.  
- Possible contributing factors include mild hay fever history and lisinopril therapy, which may cause dry cough but less likely due to concurrent nasal symptoms and systemic features.  
- The presentation is consistent primarily with a viral upper respiratory infection with possible secondary bacterial sinusitis; watchful waiting is advised with clear safety-netting.  
- Psychosocial factors including stable living situation and employment suggest no immediate psychosocial distress contributing to this presentation.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Viral upper respiratory tract infection
- Patient Goal(s): Resolution of symptoms, maintenance of hydration and diabetes control
- Clinical Goal(s): Monitor symptom progression, prevent complications especially bacterial superinfection
- Actions (Patient):  
  • Obtain and use a thermometer to monitor temperature regularly  
  • Continue supportive care (e.g., lemon drinks as soothing agents)  
  • Report worsening symptoms such as persistent fever > 37.5–38°C, increased cough severity, production of purulent sputum or blood, shortness of breath, or chest pain
- Actions (Clinician/GP):  
  • Advise on symptom monitoring and safe use of over-the-counter remedies (avoid concurrent paracetamol products with lemsip)  
  • Provide education on when to seek urgent medical review  
  • Arrange follow-up or reassessment if symptoms worsen or fail to improve after 7–10 days  
  • Reinforce maintenance of routine diabetes and blood pressure monitoring  

Secondary Problem: Possible bacterial sinusitis
- Patient Goal(s): Avoid progression to bacterial infection requiring antibiotics
- Clinical Goal(s): Early identification and treatment if bacterial sinusitis develops
- Actions (Patient): Monitor for facial pain, persistent or worsening nasal discharge, high fever
- Actions (Clinician/GP): Observation with clear safety-netting; consider antibiotics if symptoms worsen or fail to resolve

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention:
- Education Given: Yes  
  Topics Covered: Symptom management for viral infection, warning signs for bacterial infection, safe use of medications including avoiding duplicate paracetamol, importance of diabetes monitoring
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening: High or persistent fever > 37.5–38°C, worsening cough or production of sputum or blood, nasal bleeding, facial pain, shortness of breath, chest pain
- Coping Strategies: Supportive care with fluids, rest, symptom soothing agents, appropriate monitoring
